claim: Gap junctions are ubiquitous in metazoans and play critical roles in important biological processes, including electrical conduction and development.
source: Gap junctions are ubiquitous in metazoans and play critical roles in important biological processes, including electrical conduction and development.
evidence: This is a general statement about gap junctions supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Only a few defined molecules passing through gap junction channels have been linked to specific functions.
source: Yet, only a few defined molecules passing through gap junction channels have been linked to specific functions.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field regarding gap junction function.

claim: Gap junction channel mutants reduce coupling between the soma and germ cells in the Caenorhabditis elegans gonad.
source: We isolated gap junction channel mutants that reduce coupling between the soma and germ cells in the Caenorhabditis elegans gonad.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript, including genetic and phenotypic analysis.

claim: Malonyl-CoA is produced in the soma and delivered through gap junctions to the germline.
source: We provide evidence that malonyl-CoA, the rate-limiting substrate for fatty acid synthesis (FAS), is produced in the soma and delivered through gap junctions to the germline
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic mosaic analysis, transformation rescue experiments, and genetic interactions described in the manuscript.

claim: Malonyl-CoA delivered to the germline is used in fatty acid synthesis to critically support embryonic development.
source: We provide evidence that malonyl-CoA, the rate-limiting substrate for fatty acid synthesis (FAS), is produced in the soma and delivered through gap junctions to the germline; there it is used in fatty acid synthesis to critically support embryonic development.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that disruption of gap junctions or FAS genes leads to embryonic defects.

claim: Separation of malonyl-CoA production from its site of utilization facilitates somatic control of germline development.
source: Separation of malonyl-CoA production from its site of utilization facilitates somatic control of germline development.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings regarding the spatial separation of POD-2 and FASN-1 activities.

claim: Loss of malonyl-CoA production in the intestine negatively impacts germline development independently of FAS.
source: Additionally, we demonstrate that loss of malonyl-CoA production in the intestine negatively impacts germline development independently of FAS.
evidence: This is supported by genetic mosaic analysis showing that intestinal loss of pod-2 but not fasn-1 results in germline starvation-like phenotype.

claim: Metabolic outsourcing of malonyl-CoA may be a strategy by which the soma communicates nutritional status to the germline.
source: Our results suggest that metabolic outsourcing of malonyl-CoA may be a strategy by which the soma communicates nutritional status to the germline.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings regarding the role of malonyl-CoA transfer.

claim: Gap junctions are clusters of intercellular channels allowing direct passage of small molecules (<1000–2500 daltons) between coupled cells.
source: Gap junctions are clusters of intercellular channels allowing direct passage of small molecules (<1000–2500 daltons) between coupled cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap junction structure and function, supported by citation (Skerrett and Williams, 2017).

claim: Gap junctions are widespread in multicellular organisms.
source: They are widespread in multicellular organisms, although different gene families encode the protein subunits in invertebrates (innexins) and vertebrates (primarily connexins) (Skerrett and Williams, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citation.

claim: Different gene families encode gap junction protein subunits in invertebrates (innexins) and vertebrates (primarily connexins).
source: They are widespread in multicellular organisms, although different gene families encode the protein subunits in invertebrates (innexins) and vertebrates (primarily connexins) (Skerrett and Williams, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Skerrett and Williams, 2017.

claim: Identification of essential molecules that must pass through gap junction channels in vivo is challenging.
source: While the capability of small molecules to pass through gap junctions can be shown readily in cultured cells, identification of essential molecules that must pass through channels in vivo is challenging.
evidence: This reflects the current state of the field and the challenges in gap junction research.

claim: Disruption of gap junction coupling can affect cell adhesion.
source: Additionally, disruption of gap junction coupling can affect cell adhesion (Meyer et al., 1992), and resultant defects in intercellular communication may not necessarily relate to the passage of molecules through junctional channels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meyer et al., 1992.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, germ cells are coupled throughout their development to the somatic gonad by gap junctions.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, germ cells are coupled throughout their development to the somatic gonad by gap junctions (Starich et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Starich et al., 2014.

claim: Germ cells progress in assembly-line fashion through the early stages of meiosis.
source: Germ cells progress in assembly-line fashion through the early stages of meiosis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A showing the organization of the gonad.

claim: Gonadal gap junctions have been implicated in germ cell proliferation, oocyte growth, regulation of oocyte meiotic maturation, early embryogenesis and sperm guidance.
source: Gonadal gap junctions have been implicated in germ cell proliferation, oocyte growth, regulation of oocyte meiotic maturation, early embryogenesis and sperm guidance (Govindan et al., 2006; Whitten and Miller, 2007; Nadarajan et al., 2009; Edmonds et al., 2011; Starich et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Octameric gap junction hemichannels in the somatic gonad are comprised of the innexins INX-8 and INX-9.
source: Octameric gap junction hemichannels (half-channels) in the somatic gonad are comprised of the recently duplicated innexins INX-8 and INX-9
evidence: This is supported by previous characterization work and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Apposing germ cell hemichannels are heteromeric and consist of INX-14 in conjunction with either INX-21 or INX-22.
source: apposing germ cell hemichannels are heteromeric and consist of INX-14 in conjunction with either INX-21 or INX-22 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and previous characterization.

claim: Germ cells fail to proliferate in inx-8(0) inx-9(0) mutants.
source: Germ cells fail to proliferate in inx-8(0) inx-9(0) mutants, at a point upstream of, or parallel to, GLP-1/Notch activation of germ cells by Delta class ligands LAG-2 and APX-1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: LAG-2 and APX-1 are Delta class ligands produced in the distal tip cell that provides the proliferative stem cell niche.
source: These ligands are produced in the distal tip cell (DTC) that provides the proliferative stem cell niche (Austin and Kimble, 1987; Austin and Kimble, 1989; Henderson et al., 1994; Nadarajan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Ovulation in inx-8(tn1513 tn1555rf) inx-9(ok1502null) mutants is delayed ~18 hr compared to wild type.
source: Compared to the wild type (N2), ovulation in inx-8(tn1513 tn1555rf) inx-9(ok1502null) mutants (a.k.a. inx-8[rf]) is delayed ~18 hr.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B showing timing data.

claim: The inx-8(tn1513) allele encodes a T239I change in the second extracellular loop of the innexin monomer.
source: tn1513 encodes a T239I change in the second extracellular loop of the innexin monomer, predicted to be involved in docking with hemichannels on apposing cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Oshima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and structural modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tn1555 suppressor mutation encodes a D24N change in the amino terminus of INX-8.
source: One of these, tn1555, encodes a D24N change in the amino terminus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), near a site that may associate with a cytoplasmic dome structure surrounding the hemichannel outer pore (Oshima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and structural modeling.

claim: inx-8(rf) animals show partially restored germ cell numbers and fertility approximating one-third the level of wild type.
source: inx-8(rf) animals show partially restored germ cell numbers and fertility approximating one-third the level of wild type (Figure 1—source data 1; Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in the source data files.

claim: There is an ~18 hr delay to the onset of fertilization in inx-8(rf) compared to the wild type.
source: There is an ~18 hr delay to the onset of fertilization in inx-8(rf) compared to the wild type, as determined by relating the timing of first ovulation to the L4 molt (L4-to-adult transition) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by timing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: LIN-41 is the earliest known marker of oogenesis.
source: LIN-41 is the earliest known marker of oogenesis (Spike et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spike et al., 2014.

claim: In wild type at 20°C, gfp::lin41 appears by sub-stage L4.7.
source: In the wild type at 20°C, gfp::lin41 appears by sub-stage L4.7 (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1C.

claim: In inx-8(rf), gfp::lin41 is expressed after completion of vulval morphogenesis but prior to the L4 molt.
source: in inx-8(rf), gfp::lin41 is expressed after completion of vulval morphogenesis but prior to the L4 molt (Figure 1D; Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1D and quantitative data in source data 3.

claim: Spermatogenesis is delayed in inx-8(rf) mutants.
source: Spermatogenesis is also delayed—wild-type sperm appear as early as the L4.7 stage, but inx-8(rf) sperm first appear after completion of vulval morphogenesis (Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in source data 3.

claim: ~99% of inx-8(rf) progeny are laid within a 96 hr window.
source: Once started, egg-laying in inx-8(rf) continues apace such that ~99% of progeny are laid within a 96 hr window (3144/3179 larvae; n = 25), similar to the wild type (5847/5929 larvae; n = 21).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative brood analysis data.

claim: In wild-type hermaphrodites, clusters of gap junction puncta form between somatic DTC or sheath cells and each underlying germ cell.
source: In wild-type hermaphrodites, clusters of gap junction puncta form between somatic DTC or sheath cells and each underlying germ cell (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 2A.

claim: In inx-8(rf) distal arms, INX-21 and INX-22 puncta tend to localize more laterally, where the sheath cells dip down between adjacent germ cells.
source: In distal arms of the wild type, loosely clustered sheath-germ cell gap junctions form more basally on germ cells; in inx-8(rf) distal arms, both INX-21 and INX-22 puncta tend to localize more laterally, where the sheath cells dip down between adjacent germ cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 2B.

claim: In the loop region, gap junction puncta form large aggregates in wild-type animals; these are absent in inx-8(rf).
source: In the loop region (transition from meiotic pachytene to diplotene), gap junction puncta form large aggregates in wild-type animals; these are absent in inx-8(rf) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 2C.

claim: In inx-8(rf) proximal arms, INX-22 and INX-8 are strongly but diffusely expressed, with little co-localization evident.
source: In wild-type proximal arms (diakinesis), developing oocytes exhibit extensive formation of INX-22 gap junction puncta, while INX-21 puncta become faint; in inx-8(rf) proximal arms, INX-22 and INX-8 are strongly but diffusely expressed, with little co-localization evident (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 2D.

claim: There may be little gap junction coupling in inx-8(rf) proximal arms.
source: These results suggest that there may be little gap junction coupling in inx-8(rf) proximal arms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the diffuse localization pattern observed in Figure 2D.

claim: Sheath-oocyte gap junctions are endocytosed by the oocyte during ovulation.
source: We showed previously that sheath-oocyte gap junctions are endocytosed by the oocyte during ovulation (Starich et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Embryos from inx-8(0) inx-9(0) rescued with inx-8(rf)::gfp show internalized GFP puncta, confirming that inx-8(rf) establishes at least some sheath-oocyte gap junctions in the proximal arm.
source: Embryos from inx-8(0) inx-9(0) rescued with inx-8(rf)::gfp show internalized GFP puncta, confirming that inx-8(rf) establishes at least some sheath-oocyte gap junctions in the proximal arm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Delayed gametogenesis in inx-8(rf) mutants arises from compromised soma-germline gap junction communication.
source: We conclude that delayed gametogenesis in inx-8(rf) mutants arises from compromised soma-germline gap junction communication, due to altered channel properties that influence the formation and localization of gap junctions, especially in the loop and proximal arm.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunofluorescence and phenotypic data.

claim: inx-8/9 (0); Ex[inx-8(DTC+, Sh–)] produces Pod-like embryos.
source: inx-8/9 (0); Ex[inx-8(DTC+, Sh–)] produces Pod-like embryos
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observation and Table 1.

claim: At a partially restrictive temperature (22°C), fasn-1(g43ts); inx-8(rf) and emb-8(hc69ts); inx-8(rf) double mutants exhibited markedly reduced brood sizes.
source: At a partially restrictive temperature (22°C), fasn-1(g43ts); inx-8(rf) and emb-8(hc69ts); inx-8(rf) double mutants exhibited markedly reduced brood sizes.
evidence: This is supported by brood size data in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: emb-8(hc69ts) might be highly dose-sensitive to inx-8(+) levels.
source: Similar reductions in brood size were also apparent in emb-8(hc69ts); +/inx-8(rf), suggesting emb-8(hc69ts) might be highly dose-sensitive to inx-8(+) levels (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of reduced brood size in heterozygotes.

claim: pod-2(ye60cs) is rescued by simple extrachromosomal arrays at 15°C.
source: Previous characterization of pod-2 implied rescue by a simple array (Rappleye et al., 2003); we likewise found that pod-2(ye60cs) is rescued by simple extrachromosomal arrays at 15°C (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by transformation rescue experiments described in Materials and methods.

claim: Two fosmids encoding emb-8, used individually to generate simple arrays, yielded 65 transformed lines, only one of which rescued emb-8(hc69ts) at 25°C.
source: In contrast, two fosmids encoding emb-8, used individually to generate simple arrays, yielded 65 transformed lines, only one of which rescued emb-8(hc69ts) at 25°C; the array in this line was eventually silenced.
evidence: This is supported by transformation rescue experiments.

claim: Two fosmids used to generate 93 simple array lines and 20 complex array lines failed to rescue fasn-1(g43ts).
source: For fasn-1, two fosmids used to generate 93 simple array lines and 20 complex array lines failed to rescue fasn-1(g43ts).
evidence: This is supported by transformation rescue experiments.

claim: FAS affecting embryonic development requires pod-2 in the soma to support a germline requirement for fasn-1 and emb-8.
source: These results were consistent with a model in which FAS affecting embryonic development requires pod-2 in the soma to support a germline requirement for fasn-1 and emb-8.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential rescue patterns of pod-2, fasn-1, and emb-8.

claim: pod-2(0) embryos from pod-2(0)/+ parents arrest late in embryogenesis (pretzel stage).
source: pod-2(0) embryos from pod-2(0)/+ parents arrest late in embryogenesis (pretzel stage; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3D.

claim: Most fasn-1(0) embryos from fasn-1(0)/+ parents exhibit signs of differentiation, and many arrest late in embryogenesis.
source: Most fasn-1(0) embryos from fasn-1(0)/+ parents exhibit signs of differentiation, and many arrest late in embryogenesis; occasional hatchlings emerge with probable hypodermal defects (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3E-G.

claim: The terminal stages of developmental progression in both pod-2(0) and fasn-1(0) embryos derived from heterozygous parents are more advanced than classic Pod embryos.
source: The terminal stages of developmental progression in both pod-2(0) and fasn-1(0) embryos derived from heterozygous parents are more advanced than classic Pod embryos, which arrest prior to signs of morphogenesis.
evidence: This is based on comparison of embryonic phenotypes.

claim: Maternal rescue by pod-2 and fasn-1 occurs for early embryonic Pod defects.
source: This indicates a maternal rescue by pod-2 and fasn-1 of the early embryonic Pod defects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that embryos from heterozygous parents develop further than expected.

claim: pod-2(0) was rescued by simple extrachromosomal arrays, supporting probable somatic function.
source: pod-2(0) was rescued by simple extrachromosomal arrays, supporting probable somatic function.
evidence: This is supported by transformation rescue experiments.

claim: Somatic but not germline function of fasn-1(0) was rescued with a simple or complex array.
source: Using a PCR-amplified genomic fragment, we were able to rescue somatic but not germline function of fasn-1(0) with a simple or complex array (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by transformation rescue experiments.

claim: Homozygous fasn-1(0); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp(+)] adults lay almost exclusively dead embryos.
source: A genetically balanced line with a complex array, fasn-1(0)/hT2; Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp(+)], segregates healthy homozygous fasn-1(0); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp(+)] adults that lay almost exclusively dead embryos (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by brood analysis data in Table 1.

claim: Many fasn-1(0); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp(+)] embryos display polarity defects (4/14 symmetric first divisions).
source: many of these display polarity defects (4/14 symmetric first divisions)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative observation of embryonic phenotypes.

claim: The fasn-1(+) PCR fragment rescues somatic fasn-1 function and is either silenced in the germline or lacks an element necessary for sufficient germline expression.
source: We conclude this fasn-1(+) PCR fragment rescues somatic fasn-1 function and is either silenced in the germline or lacks an element necessary for sufficient germline expression; in either case, a germline requirement is indicated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue pattern and embryonic phenotypes.

claim: Rescue results are consistent with a fertility requirement for pod-2 in the somatic gonad and fasn-1 in the germline.
source: In sum, rescue results are consistent with a fertility requirement for pod-2 in the somatic gonad and fasn-1 in the germline.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential rescue patterns.

claim: If inx-8 gap junctions act in the FAS pathway, it would position these junctions as possible mediators of mal-CoA transfer from POD-2 in the soma to FASN-1 in the germline.
source: If inx-8 gap junctions act in this pathway, it would position these junctions as possible mediators of mal-CoA transfer from POD-2 in the soma to FASN-1 in the germline.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the genetic data.

claim: GFP::POD-2 expression is strongest in the intestine, and prominent in the hypodermis, gonad sheath (especially proximal sheath), CAN neuron, and excretory duct.
source: GFP::POD-2 expression is strongest in the intestine, and prominent in the hypodermis, gonad sheath (especially proximal sheath), CAN neuron, and excretory duct (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: GFP-labeled FASN-1 is expressed in the hypodermis, gonad sheath (esp. proximal) and excretory duct; however, intestine and CAN neuron expression are not evident.
source: GFP is seen in the hypodermis, gonad sheath (esp. proximal) and excretory duct; however, intestine and CAN neuron expression are not evident (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 5.

claim: Neither GFP::POD-2 nor GFP-labeled FASN-1 is expressed in the DTC.
source: Neither GFP::POD-2 nor GFP-labeled FASN-1 is expressed in the DTC.
evidence: This is based on imaging data showing absence of expression in the DTC.

claim: No germline expression of GFP-tagged pod-2 or fasn-1 was detected, including by anti-GFP staining of dissected gonads.
source: No germline expression of any of these GFP-tagged genes was detected, including by anti-GFP staining of dissected gonads (Figure 4C; Figure 5C,F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figures 4C and 5C,F.

claim: GFP::POD-2 expression in embryos first appears with development of hypodermal and intestinal cells.
source: GFP::POD-2 expression in embryos first appears with development of hypodermal and intestinal cells (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4D,E.

claim: GFP::POD-2 intestinal expression decreases in response to starvation.
source: In adults, GFP::POD-2 intestinal expression was found to decrease in response to starvation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4F.

claim: The earliest detectable GFP-tagged FASN-1 in embryos appears in developing hypodermis.
source: The earliest detectable GFP-tagged FASN-1 in embryos appears in developing hypodermis (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 5D.

claim: Expression of both pod-2 and fasn-1 is consistent with primarily somatic functions.
source: Expression of both genes is consistent with primarily somatic functions, while germline fasn-1 activity may derive from low levels of maternal expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns observed.

claim: Addition of Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] dramatically increases the brood size of emb-8(hc69ts) at 22°C.
source: Addition of Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] was found to dramatically increase the brood size of emb-8(hc69ts) at 22°C.
evidence: This is supported by brood size data in Figure 6A.

claim: The increase in brood size of emb-8(hc69ts) by Ex[pod-2(+)] is dependent on INX-8 hemichannel integrity—inx-8(+) homozygotes facilitate rescue more effectively than +/inx-8(rf) heterozygotes.
source: This increase in brood size is dependent on INX-8 hemichannel integrity—inx-8(+) homozygotes facilitate rescue more effectively than +/inx-8(rf) heterozygotes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by brood size data in Figure 6A.

claim: Although heterozygous INX-8(+)/INX-8(rf) hemichannels reduce emb-8(hc69ts) rescue by enhanced mal-CoA production, cell adhesion between soma and germline does not appear to be affected.
source: Importantly, although heterozygous INX-8(+)/INX-8(rf) hemichannels reduce emb-8(hc69ts) rescue by enhanced mal-CoA production, anti-INX-8 and anti-INX-22 co-localization in emb-8(hc69ts); +/inx-8(rf) dissected gonads is indistinguishable from the wild type (Figure 2E). Therefore, cell adhesion between soma and germline does not appear to be affected in this genetic background (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2E.

claim: Expression of Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] in fasn-1(g43ts) significantly reduced brood size (p<0.01).
source: In contrast to emb-8(hc69ts), expression of Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] in fasn-1(g43ts) significantly reduced brood size (p<0.01)
evidence: This is supported by brood size data in Figure 6B.

claim: Brood size reduction in fasn-1(g43ts) by Ex[pod-2(+)] is more severe in homozygous inx-8(+) than heterozygous +/inx-8(rf) genetic backgrounds (p<0.05).
source: and brood size reduction is more severe in homozygous inx-8(+) than heterozygous +/inx-8(rf) genetic backgrounds (ρ <0.05) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by brood size data in Figure 6B.

claim: Acetyl-CoA (FA chain initiation) and mal-CoA (chain elongation) load at a common, non-selective acyl-CoA-binding site in FASN and are regarded as competitive inhibitors.
source: This result likely relates to the mechanism of FASN production of fatty acids—acetyl-CoA (FA chain initiation) and mal-CoA (chain elongation) load at a common, non-selective acyl-CoA-binding site and are regarded as competitive inhibitors (Cox and Hammes, 1983; Chang and Hammes, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cox and Hammes, 1983 and Chang and Hammes, 1990.

claim: Increasing the ratio of mal-CoA to acetyl-CoA may inhibit FASN-1 enzyme by interfering with chain initiation.
source: Increasing the ratio of mal-CoA to acetyl-CoA may inhibit FASN-1 enzyme by interfering with chain initiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism of FASN and the observed genetic interactions.

claim: Heterozygous +/inx-8(rf) channels ameliorate the inhibition of fasn-1(g43ts) by mal-CoA, likely by reducing mal-CoA transfer to the germline.
source: Importantly, heterozygous +/inx-8(rf) channels ameliorate this inhibition (Figure 6B), likely by reducing mal-CoA transfer to the germline.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data in Figure 6B.

claim: inx-8(+) hemichannels can have both a positive (emb-8) and a negative (fasn-1) genetic effect on FAS mutations which function downstream of overexpressed pod-2(+).
source: inx-8(+) hemichannels can have both a positive (emb-8) and a negative (fasn-1) genetic effect on FAS mutations which function downstream of overexpressed pod-2(+).
evidence: This is supported by the contrasting effects shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The finding that inx-8 has both positive and negative effects on downstream FAS mutations is a strong indication that inx-8 acts in the same pathway as pod-2, rather than a parallel pathway.
source: This finding is a strong indication that inx-8 acts in the same pathway as pod-2, rather than a parallel pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction patterns.

claim: The genetic results are consistent with gap junctions acting as conveyors of mal-CoA from soma to germline.
source: These results are consistent with gap junctions acting as conveyors of mal-CoA from soma to germline
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: The genetic results fit a model in which INX-8 gap junctions are positioned between pod-2 and fasn-1.
source: and they fit a model in which INX-8 gap junctions are positioned between pod-2 and fasn-1 (Figure 6C), but not downstream of fasn-1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data and pathway analysis.

claim: 17/833 adult hermaphrodites of genotype pod-2(0); Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] were identified that produced dead eggs but no viable progeny.
source: 17/833 adult hermaphrodites were identified that produced dead eggs but no viable progeny
evidence: This is quantitative data from genetic mosaic screening.

claim: Eight pod-2(0); Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] mosaic animals lost Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] from most or all gonad sheath cells.
source: Animals fell into two classes: (1) eight animals lost Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] from most or all gonad sheath cells
evidence: This is quantitative data from genetic mosaic analysis.

claim: Nine pod-2(0); Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] mosaic animals lost Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] from the intestine.
source: and (2) nine animals lost Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] from the intestine (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is quantitative data from genetic mosaic analysis.

claim: Five pod-2(0); Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] animals lost the array from all somatic gonad sheath cells and produced no viable embryos.
source: Within the first class of mosaics, five animals lost the array in all sheath cells in both gonad arms.
evidence: This is quantitative data from genetic mosaic analysis.

claim: Three pod-2(0); Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] mosaic animals exhibited a difference in phenotypic severity between gonad arms—embryos derived from one arm developed to later multicellular stages in utero.
source: Three other animals exhibited a difference in phenotypic severity between gonad arms—embryos derived from one arm developed to later multicellular stages in utero (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Differences in phenotypic severity between gonad arms were coincident with loss of the array from all sheath cells in the more severely affected arm, versus retention of the array in a single sheath cell of the better arm.
source: Differences were coincident with loss of the array from all sheath cells in the more severely affected arm, versus retention of the array in a single sheath cell of the better arm.
evidence: This is based on correlation of array retention with phenotypic severity.

claim: The focus of pod-2(0) rescue is autonomous to each gonad arm.
source: These results indicate that the focus of pod-2(0) rescue is autonomous to each gonad arm, consistent with the interpretation that pod-2 expression in the somatic sheath is essential to embryonic viability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mosaic analysis showing arm-specific effects.

claim: pod-2 expression in the somatic sheath is essential to embryonic viability.
source: These results indicate that the focus of pod-2(0) rescue is autonomous to each gonad arm, consistent with the interpretation that pod-2 expression in the somatic sheath is essential to embryonic viability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mosaic analysis.

claim: Four pod-2(0); Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] animals were identified that maintained the array in the soma but lost the array in all embryos (P4– mosaics).
source: In subsequent screening for germline (P4–) mosaics, four animals were identified that maintained the array in the soma but lost the array in all embryos (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is quantitative data from genetic mosaic screening.

claim: The terminal stages of embryonic development in P4– mosaics resembled those of pod-2(0) embryos derived from +/pod-2(0) parents, that is embryos developed to threefold or pretzel stages but failed to hatch.
source: The terminal stages of embryonic development resembled those of pod-2(0) embryos derived from +/pod-2(0) parents, that is embryos developed to threefold or pretzel stages but failed to hatch (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 7E-G.

claim: Somatic pod-2(+) supplies sufficient levels of mal-CoA to the germline not only to establish a wild-type one-cell embryo, but also to support continued development, presumably until zygotic pod-2 expression becomes adequate for completion of embryogenesis.
source: We conclude that somatic pod-2(+) supplies sufficient levels of mal-CoA to the germline not only to establish a wild-type one-cell embryo, but also to support continued development, presumably until zygotic pod-2 expression becomes adequate for completion of embryogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the P4– mosaic analysis showing later-stage embryonic arrest.

claim: Metabolites essential for embryonic development can be produced in the somatic gonad and provided to the oocyte through gap junctions.
source: These studies establish that metabolites essential for embryonic development can be produced in the somatic gonad and provided to the oocyte through gap junctions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mosaic analysis and genetic interaction data.

claim: Nine pod-2(0); Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] E(–) mosaic animals lost Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] from the intestine and produced dead embryos.
source: The other class of pod-2(0) genetic mosaics producing dead embryos in our original screen lost Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] from the intestine (E–) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is quantitative data from genetic mosaic screening.

claim: E(–) mosaic pod-2(0); Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] animals were smaller than wild type, and gonad arms were severely reduced in size.
source: E(–) mosaic animals were smaller than wild type, and gonad arms were severely reduced in size (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 8A.

claim: Only the most proximal oocytes showed appreciable growth in E(–) mosaic pod-2(0); Ex[pod-2(+); sur-5::gfp] animals.
source: Only the most proximal oocytes showed appreciable growth.
evidence: This is based on observation of gonad morphology in E(–) mosaics.

claim: E(–) mosaic gonad arms resemble those seen in gonads undergoing the oocyte starvation response, or adult reproductive diapause (ARD).
source: E(–) mosaic gonad arms resemble those seen in gonads undergoing the oocyte starvation response, or adult reproductive diapause (ARD), a process induced by starvation during the L4 larval stage proposed to maintain germline stem cells for repopulation of the gonad upon the resumption of feeding (Angelo and Van Gilst, 2009; Seidel and Kimble, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with known ARD phenotypes, supported by citations.

claim: During ARD, germline stem cells cease dividing, the gonad shrinks due to extensive apoptosis of differentiated germ cells, and growth is largely restricted to the most proximal oocyte.
source: During ARD, germline stem cells cease dividing, the gonad shrinks due to extensive apoptosis of differentiated germ cells, and growth is largely restricted to the most proximal oocyte.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ARD, supported by citations (Angelo and Van Gilst, 2009; Seidel and Kimble, 2011).

claim: The C. elegans intestine is enriched with lipid droplets, produces yolk lipoproteins and is regarded as a major site of FAS.
source: The C. elegans intestine is enriched with lipid droplets, produces yolk lipoproteins (Kimble and Sharrock, 1983) and is regarded as a major site of FAS (Watts and Ristow, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kimble and Sharrock, 1983 and Watts and Ristow, 2017.

claim: A genetic pathway in C. elegans required for intestinal apical polarity establishment leading to proper lumen formation has been described; genes in this pathway, including pod-2, encode enzymes required for glycosphingolipid synthesis.
source: A genetic pathway in C. elegans required for intestinal apical polarity establishment leading to proper lumen formation has been described; genes in this pathway, including pod-2, encode enzymes required for glycosphingolipid synthesis (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: Two presumptive P1(–) pod-2 mosaics were identified, predicted to have lost pod-2(+) function in the intestine, somatic gonad, germline, and many muscle and hypodermal cells.
source: We subsequently identified two presumptive P1(–) pod-2 mosaics, predicted to have lost pod-2(+) function in the intestine, somatic gonad, germline, and many muscle and hypodermal cells, among others (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is quantitative data from genetic mosaic screening.

claim: The most striking phenotype distinguishing P1(–) mosaics from E(–) mosaics was an extremely constipated intestine.
source: The most striking phenotype distinguishing these animals from E(–) mosaics was an extremely constipated intestine (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 8B.

claim: The absence of constipation in E(–) mosaic animals implies that loss of pod-2(+) from the intestine does not prevent the processing of bacteria through the intestinal lumen.
source: Therefore the absence of this constipation in E(–) mosaic animals implies that loss of pod-2(+) from the intestine does not prevent the processing of bacteria through the intestinal lumen.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of E(–) and P1(–) mosaic phenotypes.

claim: Ten fasn-1(0); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp] E(–) mosaic animals were identified.
source: Ten (of 800) such animals were identified (Figure 7A)
evidence: This is quantitative data from genetic mosaic screening.

claim: In contrast to pod-2, fasn-1(0); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp] E(–) mosaic animals' gonad arms appeared normal.
source: in stark contrast to pod-2, their gonad arms appeared normal.
evidence: This is based on observation of gonad morphology in fasn-1 E(–) mosaics.

claim: fasn-1(0); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp] E(–) mosaic animals displayed no overt defects outside of Pod embryo production.
source: These animals displayed no overt defects outside of Pod embryo production (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 8C.

claim: There is no significant intestinal requirement for zygotic fasn-1 in larval and adult stages.
source: However, the surprising conclusion from this mosaic analysis is that there is no significant intestinal requirement for zygotic fasn-1 in larval and adult stages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the normal appearance of fasn-1 E(–) mosaics.

claim: The primary function of mal-CoA produced in the intestine is not as substrate for intestinal FASN-1.
source: The implication is that the primary function of mal-CoA produced in the intestine is not as substrate for intestinal FASN-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the contrasting phenotypes of pod-2 and fasn-1 E(–) mosaics.

claim: inx-8(rf) and inx-8/9(0); Ex[inx-8(DTC+, Sh–)] mutants share delayed oogenesis and a reduction in gap junction coupling, germ cell proliferation, and brood size.
source: inx-8(rf) and inx-8/9(0); Ex[inx-8(DTC+, Sh–)] mutants share delayed oogenesis and a reduction in gap junction coupling, germ cell proliferation, and brood size (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1 and previous figures.

claim: inx-21(0) mutants are sterile.
source: inx-21(0) mutants are sterile, and inx-22(0) mutants are fertile (Starich et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Starich et al., 2014.

claim: inx-22(0) mutants are fertile.
source: inx-21(0) mutants are sterile, and inx-22(0) mutants are fertile (Starich et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Starich et al., 2014.

claim: Mal-CoA required for embryonic development must minimally transit through gap junction channels composed of INX-14/INX-21 germline hemichannels.
source: therefore, mal-CoA required for embryonic development must minimally transit through gap junction channels composed of INX-14/INX-21 germline hemichannels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sterility of inx-21(0) mutants and fertility of inx-22(0) mutants.

claim: Lower copy number rescue of pod-2(0) coincided with reduced embryo output (84% of wild-type) and lower proportion of viable larvae within a brood (~37% of total embryos).
source: Lower copy number rescue coincided with reduced embryo output (84% of wild-type) and lower proportion of viable larvae within a brood (~37% of total embryos) (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Somatically rescued fasn-1(0); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp] embryo output is comparable to the wild type (94%).
source: Somatically rescued fasn-1(0); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp] embryo output is comparable to the wild type (94%), consistent with a minimal role for germline fasn-1 in promoting embryo output.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Embryo output in the fasn-1(0); inx-8(rf); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp] double mutant is reduced to ~50% of inx-8(rf) alone.
source: Further, we observed that embryo output in the fasn-1(0); inx-8(rf); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp] double mutant is reduced to ~50% of inx-8(rf) alone (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: inx-8(rf) partially suppresses the embryonic lethality of fasn-1(0); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp] such that fasn-1(0); inx-8(rf); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp] strains can be maintained as viable and fertile lines with low brood sizes.
source: Surprisingly, inx-8(rf) partially suppresses the embryonic lethality of fasn-1(0); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp] such that fasn-1(0); inx-8(rf); Ex[fasn-1(+); sur-5::gfp] strains can be maintained as viable and fertile lines with low brood sizes (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Mal-CoA produced in the somatic sheath is delivered through gap junctions to the germline.
source: The genetic analysis of mutant inx-8 soma-germline gap junction channels has led us to three conclusions that have significance beyond the C. elegans model system. First, mal-CoA produced in the somatic sheath is delivered through gap junctions to the germline (Figure 9)
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by genetic mosaic analysis, transformation rescue, and genetic interactions.

claim: Somatically derived mal-CoA is necessary to establish a proper one-cell embryo and to support continued embryogenesis.
source: somatically derived mal-CoA is necessary to establish a proper one-cell embryo and to support continued embryogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by genetic mosaic analysis showing that somatic pod-2 can support embryonic development.

claim: The contrasting responses of fasn-1(g43ts) and emb-8(hc69ts) to over-expression of pod-2(+) in the context of mutant INX-8 hemichannels strongly support a model positioning gap junctions between pod-2 and fasn-1.
source: The contrasting responses of fasn-1(g43ts) and emb-8(hc69ts) to over-expression of pod-2(+) in the context of mutant INX-8 hemichannels, strongly support a model positioning gap junctions between pod-2 and fasn-1 (Figure 9).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data in Figure 6.

claim: Mal-CoA is a hydrophilic, membrane impermeable molecule of a size (854 daltons) which is well within the range known to traverse the aqueous pore size of innexin gap junctions (~20–30 Å or up to ~2500 daltons).
source: Mal-CoA produced by POD-2 is a hydrophilic, membrane impermeable molecule of a size (854 daltons) which is well within the range known to traverse the aqueous pore size of innexin gap junctions (~20–30 Å or up to ~2500 daltons; Skerrett and Williams, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by knowledge of mal-CoA properties and citation to Skerrett and Williams, 2017.

claim: Palmitate and downstream fatty acids can cross cell membranes.
source: In contrast, palmitate and downstream fatty acids can cross cell membranes (Schwenk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwenk et al., 2010.

claim: Palmitate added to the media can rescue one-cell polarity, but not osmotic integrity, in pod-2(ye60cs) embryos.
source: Indeed, palmitate added to the media was shown to rescue one-cell polarity, but not osmotic integrity, in pod-2(ye60cs) embryos (Rappleye et al., 2003), suggesting that dietary palmitate can traffic from the intestine to the gonad
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rappleye et al., 2003.

claim: Dietary palmitate can traffic from the intestine to the gonad.
source: suggesting that dietary palmitate can traffic from the intestine to the gonad
evidence: This is an inference based on the palmitate rescue experiment cited.

claim: pod-2 expression (and presumably mal-CoA production) is exceptionally robust in the intestine and essential for normal germline development.
source: Second, pod-2 expression (and presumably mal-CoA production) is exceptionally robust in the intestine and essential for normal germline development.
evidence: This is supported by GFP expression data and E(–) mosaic analysis.

claim: In the absence of intestinal POD-2, the germline exhibits phenotypic hallmarks of the germline ARD response despite the presence of a replete food source.
source: In the absence of intestinal POD-2, the germline exhibits phenotypic hallmarks of the germline ARD response despite the presence of a replete food source.
evidence: This is supported by observation of E(–) mosaic phenotypes.

claim: Intestinal fasn-1 expression is not similarly required as pod-2.
source: By contrast, intestinal fasn-1 expression is not similarly required.
evidence: This is supported by the normal appearance of fasn-1 E(–) mosaics.

claim: The primordial germ cells Z2 and Z3 associate with a pair of intestinal cells during embryogenesis, but these contacts are lost before hatching.
source: At least one additional route may deliver mal-CoA to the germline early in its development—the primordial germ cells Z2 and Z3 associate with a pair of intestinal cells during embryogenesis, but these contacts are lost before hatching (Sulston et al., 1983; Abdu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sulston et al., 1983 and Abdu et al., 2016.

claim: An early germline requirement for mal-CoA could be fulfilled directly from the intestine.
source: Therefore, an early germline requirement for mal-CoA could be fulfilled directly from the intestine; loss of such a function would be encompassed within the ARD-like phenotype seen in pod-2 E(–) mosaics.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known contact between primordial germ cells and intestine.

claim: The HLH-30/TEFB transcription factor functions as a master regulator of the ARD state.
source: Recent results show that the HLH-30/TEFB transcription factor functions as a master regulator of the ARD state (Gerisch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerisch et al., 2020.

claim: hlh-30 mutants fail to effect the system-wide changes promoting long-term survival and recovery associated with ARD.
source: hlh-30 mutants fail to effect the system-wide changes promoting long-term survival and recovery associated with ARD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerisch et al., 2020.

claim: Entry of hlh-30 mutants into the ARD state appears normal.
source: However, entry of hlh-30 mutants into the ARD state appears normal.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerisch et al., 2020.

claim: A pronounced delay in gametogenesis along with reduction in brood size results from reduced soma-germline gap junction communication.
source: Third, a pronounced delay in gametogenesis along with reduction in brood size results from reduced soma-germline gap junction communication
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic analysis of inx-8(rf) mutants.

claim: Results indicating that somatic mal-CoA transits from somatic sheath to the germline via gap junctions are consistent with other findings in C. elegans related to fatty acid metabolism in oocytes, particularly a strict requirement for PUFA synthesis.
source: Our results indicating that somatic mal-CoA transits from somatic sheath to the germline via gap junctions are consistent with other findings in C. elegans related to fatty acid metabolism in oocytes, particularly a strict requirement for PUFA synthesis (Watts et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Watts et al., 2018.

claim: PUFA-dependent prostaglandin signaling from developing oocytes influences sperm guidance, and reduction of inx-14 function disrupts this signaling.
source: PUFA-dependent prostaglandin signaling from developing oocytes influences sperm guidance, and reduction of inx-14 function disrupts this signaling (Kubagawa et al., 2006; Edmonds et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kubagawa et al., 2006 and Edmonds et al., 2011.

claim: Lower levels of mal-CoA delivered to the oogenic germline through mutant INX-14-containing gap junctions reduce prostaglandin synthesis and its signaling function for sperm migration.
source: We suggest that lower levels of mal-CoA delivered to the oogenic germline through mutant INX-14-containing gap junctions reduce prostaglandin synthesis and its signaling function for sperm migration.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known role of PUFAs in prostaglandin signaling and the effect of inx-14 mutations.

claim: The segregation of the cellular source of mal-CoA from the eventual cell type in which it is used as substrate is novel.
source: To our knowledge, this segregation of the cellular source of mal-CoA from the eventual cell type in which it is used as substrate is novel.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: As the rate-limiting step in FAS, mal-CoA production is an attractive control point to tie aspects of germ cell developmental progression to somatic control.
source: As the rate-limiting step in FAS, mal-CoA production is an attractive control point to tie aspects of germ cell developmental progression to somatic control.
evidence: This is speculation about the biological significance of the findings.

claim: Cytoplasmic FAS is carried out by a multifunctional megasynthase like that encoded by fasn-1 (type-I system).
source: Cytoplasmic FAS is carried out by a multifunctional megasynthase like that encoded by fasn-1 (type-I system).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FAS systems.

claim: Mitochondria carry out FAS independently using monofunctional enzymes resembling the bacterial FAS type-II system.
source: Mitochondria carry out FAS independently using monofunctional enzymes resembling the bacterial FAS type-II system (recently reviewed by Kastaniotis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Kastaniotis et al., 2017.

claim: Mitochondrial FAS utilizes an acyl-carrier protein rather than CoA to shuttle the substrate between enzymes.
source: Mitochondrial FAS utilizes an acyl-carrier protein rather than CoA to shuttle the substrate between enzymes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial FAS.

claim: An ACC enzyme has been found in the mitochondria of S. cerevisiae but not mammals.
source: An ACC enzyme has been found in the mitochondria of S. cerevisiae but not mammals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial ACC.

claim: In mammals, the ACSF3 enzyme uses malonate as a substrate to synthesize mal-CoA and could contribute to mitochondrial FAS.
source: In mammals, the ACSF3 enzyme uses malonate as a substrate to synthesize mal-CoA and could contribute to mitochondrial FAS.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ACSF3 function.

claim: Malonate is a toxic metabolite that inhibits succinate dehydrogenase.
source: However, malonate is a toxic metabolite that inhibits succinate dehydrogenase
evidence: This is established knowledge about malonate.

claim: Knockout of ACSF3 in cultured cells suggests this enzyme is more critical for eliminating toxic malonate from mitochondria rather than serving an essential function for mitochondrial FAS.
source: and knockout of ACSF3 in cultured cells suggests this enzyme is more critical for eliminating toxic malonate from mitochondria rather than serving an essential function for mitochondrial FAS (Bowman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bowman et al., 2017.

claim: It has been suggested that hydrolysis of cytosolic mal-CoA may produce malonate that is taken up by mitochondria.
source: The sources of malonate and mal-CoA in mitochondria are still unclear, although it has been suggested that hydrolysis of cytosolic mal-CoA may produce malonate that is taken up by mitochondria (Bowman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bowman et al., 2017.

claim: Reduced levels of cytoplasmic mal-CoA could negatively impact mitochondrial FAS.
source: If this is the case, reduced levels of cytoplasmic mal-CoA could negatively impact mitochondrial FAS.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed relationship between cytoplasmic mal-CoA and mitochondrial malonate.

claim: Mal-CoA has established roles as a regulatory molecule.
source: In addition to its metabolic function in FAS, mal-CoA has established roles as a regulatory molecule.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mal-CoA function.

claim: Mal-CoA inhibits uptake and therefore oxidation of fatty acyl-CoAs by carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-1).
source: It inhibits uptake and therefore oxidation of fatty acyl-CoAs by carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mal-CoA regulation of CPT-1.

claim: Beta-oxidation of fatty acids in mitochondria provides energy through oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Beta-oxidation of fatty acids in mitochondria provides energy through oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fatty acid metabolism.

claim: The inhibitory mal-CoA in some tissues that exhibit low levels of FAS (heart and skeletal) derives from a second acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC2), which associates with the mitochondrial membrane to produce mal-CoA regulating CPT-1.
source: The inhibitory mal-CoA in some tissues that exhibit low levels of FAS (heart and skeletal) derives from a second acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC2), which associates with the mitochondrial membrane to produce mal-CoA regulating CPT-1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ACC2 function.

claim: Manipulation of mal-CoA levels in the mouse hypothalamus regulates food intake.
source: Manipulation of mal-CoA levels in the mouse hypothalamus regulates food intake (Wolfgang and Lane, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wolfgang and Lane, 2006.

claim: Regulation of food intake by mal-CoA is effected through the brain-specific CPT1-c, via a mechanism distinct from the enzymatic activity of other CPT1 enzymes.
source: Regulation is effected through the brain-specific CPT1-c, via a mechanism distinct from the enzymatic activity of other CPT1 enzymes (Sierra et al., 2008; Reilly and Mak, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sierra et al., 2008 and Reilly and Mak, 2012.

claim: Malonylation as a post-translational lysine modification has recently been described.
source: Malonylation as a post-translational lysine modification has recently been described (Peng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peng et al., 2011.

claim: Malonylation may inhibit target proteins, such as the glycolytic enzymes glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase and pyruvate kinase.
source: Malonylation may inhibit target proteins, such as the glycolytic enzymes glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase and pyruvate kinase (Kulkarni et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kulkarni et al., 2017.

claim: ACSF3 was shown to be essential for malonylation of mitochondrial protein targets.
source: and ACSF3 was shown to be essential for malonylation of mitochondrial protein targets (Bowman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bowman et al., 2017.

claim: Malonylation of mTOR reduces mTORC1 complex activity, decreasing endothelial cell proliferation and reducing angiogenesis in a human umbilical model.
source: Malonylation of mTOR reduces mTORC1 complex activity, decreasing endothelial cell proliferation and reducing angiogenesis in a human umbilical model (Bruning et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bruning et al., 2018.

claim: One trait associated with rapid tumor growth is an increase in FAS, and FASN has been explored as a cancer therapy target.
source: Finally, we note that one trait associated with rapid tumor growth is an increase in FAS, and FASN has been explored as a cancer therapy target (Menendez and Lupu, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Menendez and Lupu, 2007.

claim: The ability of mal-CoA to transit through gap junctions might sustain FAS during tumor progression.
source: Possibly, the ability of mal-CoA to transit through gap junctions might sustain FAS during tumor progression.
evidence: This is speculation about potential implications of the findings for cancer biology.

claim: The discovery that mal-CoA transits through gap junctions from soma to germline may be indicative of other unappreciated intercellular roles for this important molecule.
source: The discovery that mal-CoA transits through gap junctions from soma to germline may be indicative of other unappreciated intercellular roles for this important molecule.
evidence: This is speculation about broader implications of the findings.
